request:
Keep keyword before leading-dot float literal (issue601)

The SQL_REGEX rule that tags a word followed by a period as a Name (to
support ``schema . name`` member access) also matched a keyword sitting in
front of a float literal written without a leading zero, e.g. the ``BETWEEN``
in ``x BETWEEN .03 AND .06``. As a result BETWEEN was demoted to a Name, the
statement was grouped incorrectly, and the bounds were no longer standalone
number tokens.

Add a ``(?!\d)`` negative lookahead so the Name-before-period rule ignores a
period that starts a numeric literal, while ``schema . name`` grouping is
preserved. Adds regression tests covering both the fix and the member-access
behavior.

request:
Fix get_real_name for names with more than two dotted parts (#332)

get_real_name anchored on the first dot (via token_next_by), so it
returned the second component of a fully-qualified name. For a 2-part
name the first dot is also the last, so it was accidentally correct;
for 3+ parts it returned an intermediate component:

    parse("db.schema.tbl.col")[0].tokens[0].get_real_name()
    # 'schema', should be 'col'

The object name is the component after the last dot. Anchor on the last
dot instead. get_parent_name still uses the first dot, as documented, so
parent/real name now come from opposite ends as intended.

request:
Issue 1284: don't let a bucket lookup invent a key

bucket._cache was a defaultdict(deque), and _get_values opened with
`if self._cache[value]:` — a read that inserts an empty deque on a miss.
__iter__ reports `iter(self._cache)`, so every failed lookup left a
permanent phantom key behind, and __contains__ routes through
_get_values, so a plain `in` test was enough to create one.

The result was that `'c' in s` and `'c' in list(s)` disagreed for the
same object at the same moment, misses accumulated, and the docstring's
own "Get the keys" example returned a fourth key after one membership
test.

Make _cache a plain dict so a lookup cannot insert, and register a key
only where an item with that key is actually seen. A key whose items are
produced straight to the caller is registered at that point, so the
existing test_list case — a key fully consumed through s[key] is still
listed — keeps working.

request:
Fix one()/only() dropping a falsy user-supplied exception

`one(it, too_long=exc)` and `only(it, too_long=exc)` used
`raise too_long or ValueError(msg)`, so a `too_long`/`too_short` whose
instances are falsy (e.g. an Exception subclass overriding `__bool__`)
was discarded and the default `ValueError` raised instead.

Switch to explicit `is not None` checks, and only build the default
message when no custom exception is supplied so a faulty `__repr__` on
the iterable's items can't shadow the requested exception.

request:
Limit number of parts of a key (#286)

* Limit number of parts of a key

tomli has quadratic time complexity when handling parts of a key
(via Flags.is_ calls in key_value_rule's loop, and maybe elsewhere).
This isn't a problem unless a document has an excessive number (10_000-ish)
of parts in a key. Limiting input seems like the best fix here.

`sys.getrecursionlimit` and `RecursionError` is already (and in the non-mypyc
version, implicitly) used for `MAX_INLINE_NESTING`.
Keys aren't parsed recursively, but that's an implementation detail;
`RecursionError` works nicely for names recursive structures.
